lead: A fuselage in flight is a thin-walled tube doing two jobs at once: it holds cabin pressure and it bends like a beam. The tail unit hangs off its rear end, and the tailplane and fin loads feed bending and twist into that beam. Stress analysis asks what stresses meet at each point and whether they pass the material check. It is the part of this subject that exams most often ask with numbers.
prereq: You need: the load factor from Loads on aircraft and design considerations, the corner points of the V-n diagram, and shear and moment diagrams from Shear force and bending moment distribution on wings.

sections.h3: The fuselage as a pressure tube and a beam

blocks.text: Cabin pressure p is a differential pressure: inside absolute pressure minus outside ambient pressure. On a thin circular cylinder of mean radius r and skin thickness t, it gives two membrane stresses at right angles:
σ<sub>h</sub> = p r / t    σ<sub>l</sub> = p r / (2t)
blocks.where: σ<sub>h</sub> is the hoop stress round the circumference and σ<sub>l</sub> the longitudinal stress along the axis, both in Pa; p is in Pa; r and t are in m.

blocks.text: Hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress, so a fatigue crack in plain skin tends to run along the fuselage. The tube is also a beam: a bending moment M gives an axial stress σ<sub>b</sub> = M y / I. For a thin circular tube I ≈ π r³ t, and the skin sits at y = r. Stringers add area far from the neutral axis, so a stiffened section is often treated as a tube with an equivalent thickness: skin plus the stringer area spread round the circumference.

sections.h3: Fuselage bending and the tail balancing load

blocks.text: Treat the fuselage as a beam held at the wing. At load factor n, every mass m aft of a frame pushes down with n m g, and the tailplane load P acts at the tail. The bending moment at a frame is each load times its distance from the frame, so the rear-fuselage moment is zero at the tail and grows forward to its largest value at the wing attachment, where the carry-through reacts it.

The tail load comes from pitch balance. The wing lift L<sub>w</sub> acts a distance a behind the centre of gravity (CG), the wing has a nose-down pitching moment M₀, and the tail load P (upward positive) acts l<sub>t</sub> behind the CG. Moments about the CG and vertical equilibrium give:
P = −(n W a + M₀) / (l<sub>t</sub> − a)    L<sub>w</sub> = n W − P
blocks.where: W is the weight in N; a and l<sub>t</sub> are in m; M₀ is in N·m. A negative P is a download.

blocks.text: This is how the V-n diagram sizes the tail and fuselage: each corner gives n and a speed; the speed sets M₀, which grows with dynamic pressure; the formula gives P. The largest balancing loads usually come at VA and VD. The tailplane is itself a cantilever, so its own bending moment peaks at the tailplane root.

sections.h3: Fin loads and local load paths

blocks.text: The fin carries a side load F from rudder or sideslip at a height h above the fuselage axis. The fuselage receives a sideways bending moment and a torque T = F h, which the closed skin carries as a constant shear flow q = T / (2A), A being the area the skin encloses; torsion of closed sections derives this later.

items: Frames take concentrated loads (floor beams, wing, gear and tail fittings) and spread them into the skin as shear.
A domed pressure bulkhead carries pressure as membrane tension; a flat one bends and is much heavier.
A window or door cut-out breaks the hoop load path, so a doubler or surround frame carries the lost load, with rounded corners.

blocks.text: Hoop and longitudinal stresses act on perpendicular faces, so they are not simply added. For ductile aluminium, use von Mises with the total longitudinal stress σ<sub>x</sub>, pressure plus or minus bending:
σ<sub>vm</sub> = √(σ<sub>x</sub>² − σ<sub>x</sub> σ<sub>h</sub> + σ<sub>h</sub>²),   σ<sub>x</sub> = p r/(2t) ± M y/I
blocks.where: σ<sub>vm</sub> is the equivalent stress in Pa; + applies on the tension side of the bend, − on the compression side.

blocks.text: Compare limit-load stresses with yield and ultimate-load stresses with ultimate strength. A compressive σ<sub>x</sub> must also pass a skin and stringer buckling check.

examples.question: A fuselage has mean radius 1.2 m and skin 1.6 mm thick. Cabin differential pressure is 55 kPa and the ultimate bending moment at a section is 200 kN·m. The skin is 2024-T3 (yield about 345 MPa, ultimate about 485 MPa). Treat the section as a plain skin tube. Find σ<sub>h</sub>, σ<sub>l</sub>, I, σ<sub>b</sub>, the total σ<sub>x</sub> on each side of the bend and the von Mises stress, and comment on the margin.
steps: Tension side: σ<sub>x</sub> = 20.63 + 27.63 = 48.26 MPa. Compression side: σ<sub>x</sub> = 20.63 − 27.63 = −7.01 MPa.

σ<sub>vm</sub> = √(48.26² − 48.26 × 41.25 + 41.25²) = √2039.6 = 45.16 MPa. The compression side gives the same 45.16 MPa, because the two values of σ<sub>x</sub> sit equally either side of σ<sub>h</sub>/2.

Margin: 45.2 MPa at ultimate load is far below 485 MPa; at limit load (÷ 1.5) it is about 30 MPa, far below the 345 MPa yield. The −7.0 MPa side still needs a buckling check, and pressure fatigue is checked separately.
examples.answer: σ<sub>h</sub> = 41.25 MPa, σ<sub>l</sub> = 20.63 MPa, I = 8.686 × 10⁻³ m⁴, σ<sub>b</sub> = 27.63 MPa, σ<sub>x</sub> = 48.26 and −7.01 MPa, σ<sub>vm</sub> = 45.2 MPa on both sides. Static strength passes easily; buckling and fatigue decide the design.

examples.question: An airliner of weight W = 500 kN pulls up at n = 2.5. The wing lift acts a = 0.5 m behind the CG, the wing pitching moment is M₀ = 150 kN·m nose-down, and the tailplane load acts l<sub>t</sub> = 15 m behind the CG. (a) Find the tail load and the wing lift. (b) The tail unit has a mass of 800 kg at the tail load line. Find the bending moment at a frame 10 m forward of the tail, and the bending stress there for a stiffened tube of mean radius 1.2 m with an equivalent thickness of 3.0 mm. Take g = 9.81 m/s².
steps: Tail inertia: n m g = 2.5 × 800 × 9.81 = 19.62 kN downward, so the load aft of the frame is 53.45 + 19.62 = 73.07 kN.
Moment at the frame: M = 73.07 × 10 = 730.7 kN·m, top of the fuselage in tension.
examples.answer: P = −53.45 kN (download) and L<sub>w</sub> = 1303.45 kN. At the frame M = 730.7 kN·m, giving ±53.8 MPa (top in tension). A full check also adds the inertia of the rear-fuselage structure and payload aft of the frame.

traps: Adding hoop stress straight into the longitudinal total. They act at right angles; combine them with von Mises.
Drawing the rear-fuselage moment largest at the tail. It is zero at the tail and grows forward to the wing; only the tailplane’s own moment peaks at its root.
Forgetting the tail mass’s inertia: at n = 2.5 an 800 kg tail adds 19.6 kN to the download.
Using absolute cabin pressure instead of differential pressure. At 11 km the outside pressure is about 23 kPa, so a cabin held near 75 kPa absolute is loaded by about 52 kPa.
Using π r⁴/4 for a thin tube. The thin-tube value is I ≈ π r³ t.

quiz.q: State the two membrane stresses in a pressurised thin cylinder and their ratio.
quiz.a: σ<sub>h</sub> = p r / t and σ<sub>l</sub> = p r / (2t); hoop stress is twice the longitudinal stress.

quiz.q: Why is the rear-fuselage bending moment largest at the wing attachment and not at the tail?
quiz.a: The tail load and the inertia of masses aft of a frame act at the tail end. Moment is load times distance, so it is zero at the tail and grows forward to the wing attachment, where the carry-through reacts it.

quiz.q: In level flight (n = 1) the aircraft of worked example 2 has the same a, M₀ and l<sub>t</sub>. Find the tail load and the wing lift.
A fin side load of 30 kN acts 2.5 m above the axis of a fuselage of mean radius 1.2 m and skin 1.6 mm. Find the fuselage torque and the skin shear stress.
A thin cylinder has mean radius 0.9 m, skin 2 mm and differential pressure 60 kPa. Find the hoop and longitudinal stresses.
A tailplane balancing load reverses from downward to upward. What changes in the rear-fuselage stresses?
quiz.a: The bending moment changes sign, so the tension and compression sides swap. Each side sees alternating stress, and the side now in compression needs a buckling check, so the load spectrum must include both directions.

beyond: Not for the exam. In industry, fuselage stresses come from finite element models of the skin-stringer-frame structure, with pressure, inertia and tail loads as load cases, and local models for window corners and fitting lugs. Search for fuselage idealisation, tail load balancing and fin root fitting loads.
